title: God the Righteous Judge
superscription: A Shiggaion of David, which he sang to the LORD concerning the words of Cush, a Benjamite.

verses.text: O LORD my God, I take refuge in You; save me and deliver me from all my pursuers,
or they will shred my soul like a lion and tear me to pieces with no one to rescue me.
O LORD my God, if I have done this, if injustice is on my hands,
if I have rewarded my ally with evil, if I have plundered my foe without cause,
then may my enemy pursue me and overtake me; may he trample me to the ground and leave my honor in the dust. Selah
Arise, O LORD, in Your anger; rise up against the fury of my enemies. Awake, my God, and ordain judgment.
Let the assembled peoples gather around You; take Your seat over them on high.
The LORD judges the peoples; vindicate me, O LORD, according to my righteousness and integrity.
Put an end to the evil of the wicked, but establish the righteous, O righteous God who searches hearts and minds.
My shield is with God, who saves the upright in heart.
God is a righteous judge and a God who feels indignation each day.
If one does not repent, God will sharpen His sword; He has bent and strung His bow.
He has prepared His deadly weapons; He ordains His arrows with fire.
Behold, the wicked man travails with evil; he conceives trouble and births falsehood.
He has dug a hole and hollowed it out; he has fallen into a pit of his own making.
His trouble recoils on himself, and his violence falls on his own head.
I will thank the LORD for His righteousness and sing praise to the name of the LORD Most High.

context.author: The title says “of David” (Hebrew le-David), which can mean by David, for David or about David. Seventy-three psalms carry his name; tradition and the New Testament take many of them as his.
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship in Jerusalem, and every reader who prays
context.setting: The title says David sang it “concerning the words of Cush, a Benjamite,” a man not otherwise known. Falsely accused, David takes refuge in God (v.1) and puts himself on oath: if he has done wrong, let his enemy trample him (vv.3-5). Then he calls the LORD to rise up and judge: “vindicate me, O LORD, according to my righteousness and integrity” (v.8), for God “searches hearts and minds” (v.9) and “is a righteous judge” (v.11). The wicked man conceives trouble and falls into the pit he dug (vv.14-16). David ends with thanks to “the LORD Most High” (v.17).
context.custom: A shiggaion (title) may be a song of strong emotion or a lament; the word is rare and uncertain. An accused person could clear himself by an oath of innocence, calling down a curse on himself if guilty (vv.3-5; Numbers 5:19-22; Job 31). Benjamin was Saul’s tribe, and many Benjamites stayed loyal to Saul’s house against David (2 Samuel 16:5-8).
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 8 lifts our eyes to the heavens: “What is man that You are mindful of him?”
context.timelineBible: Christ calls Himself “the One who searches minds and hearts” (Revelation 2:23), as God does in v.9. The pit-digger who falls into his own trap (v.15) comes again in Psalm 9:15 and Proverbs 26:27. Shimei, a Benjamite of Saul’s family, cursed David as he fled (2 Samuel 16:5-8).

translation.meaning: To judge, govern, set right. God judges the peoples.
The Most High, a title of God as supreme over all (Genesis 14:18-20).

gospelParallels.note: I am He who searches minds and hearts.
The righteous Judge will award the crown.
He entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly.

otBackground.note: Melchizedek, priest of God Most High.
He who digs a pit will fall into it.

overview.summary: Falsely accused, David swears his innocence, calls on God the righteous Judge, and sees the wicked fall into their own pit.
overview.settingLine: A man falsely accused before God’s court.

history.t: Unknown; perhaps one of Saul’s supporters.

customs.t: Calling down a curse if guilty.
A rare word, perhaps an emotional song.

archaeology.t: Saul’s hometown in Benjamin, north of Jerusalem (Tell el-Ful).
Bronze and iron arrowheads are common Iron Age finds.

overview.discussion: David brings his case to God instead of taking revenge (vv.6-9). Where do I need to leave my vindication with God?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (1-80 in the app so far). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: David

historicalImage.caption: King David Playing the Harp, by Gerard van Honthorst (1622, Centraal Museum, Utrecht). Seventy-three psalms carry David’s name in their titles, and 1 Samuel 16:23 remembers him as a skilled player of the lyre.

currentImage.caption: The Stepped Stone Structure on the City of David, the hill David captured and made his capital (2 Samuel 5:6-9). Many archaeologists date it to the 10th or 9th century BC; the dating is debated.
